segments.say: If you'd like to, you can make yourself comfortable now. Let your shoulders drop a little. Let your hands rest wherever they are. There's nothing more to learn tonight, and nothing you need to remember.
Before we slow right down, here is one last small story, and it's a sleepy one. It's about a video game, and it's one of my favourite findings in this whole subject.

In 2000, Robert Stickgold and colleagues asked volunteers to play the falling-blocks game Tetris for about seven hours, spread over three days. As the volunteers drifted off to sleep, many of them reported seeing the falling shapes, drifting through the dark. Some even felt the shapes turning, as if they were still playing.

show.what: Had people play the game Tetris for hours, then asked what they saw as they fell asleep

segments.say: Then came the surprise. The team also asked people with severe amnesia, who could not remember playing the game at all, to play it. And some of them also reported seeing falling shapes as they fell asleep, though they couldn't say where the pictures had come from. The sleeping brain was replaying something the waking mind could not recall.

It's a lovely thought to carry into the night. Your brain is quietly working on the day, whether or not you can say what it is doing. You don't have to supervise it. You don't have to try. It knows how.
Imagine a small, steady light somewhere in the room. It doesn't flicker. It doesn't need anything from you. It's just there, warm and calm, while the rest of the room fades gently into the dark.

Now, if you like, we can borrow the oldest memory trick there is, and use it for something gentler. Imagine you are standing at the front door of a house you know well. It could be a home from long ago, or the one you live in now. There's no need to get the details right.

You open the door, slowly. The hall is quiet. There might be a soft light on, or a pale glow from a window. You take one slow step inside, and then another, and notice how little is asked of you here. Nothing needs to be carried. Nothing needs to be remembered.

In the next room, there is a chair, and a lamp, turned low. You walk past it, quietly. In the one after that, a window, and the sound of rain, or wind, or perhaps nothing at all. Each room is a little warmer than the last, and a little darker, and a little quieter.

And at the end of the house, there's a room with a bed, or a sofa, or a deep soft chair, whichever you would like most. You walk in, and you settle. Everything you carried in with you today, you can leave by the door.
Let's notice the breath for a moment. Breathing in, slowly. And breathing out, a little longer. In. And out. Your body knows how to do this on its own. You can simply watch.

Now, if you'd like, picture a room you know well. Perhaps a room from long ago, or the one you're in now. You don't have to make it exact. Whatever your mind offers is fine. A chair. A window. A soft light. Your mind is building it right now, without any effort at all.

There are no facts to keep tonight. No names to recall. No dates to check. Just the room, and the breath. If a thought about tomorrow arrives, you can let it float by, like a leaf on a pond, and let it drift on.

show.title: Nothing to hold on to
items: Just the room, and the breath

segments.say: Think of today as it was. A few moments from the morning. A few from the afternoon. Whatever you ate, whoever you spoke to. You don't need to sort them. Your brain will do that, in its own time, tonight. Some will stay. Some will fade. Both are fine.

If you notice yourself trying to remember something you forgot today, you can set it down. It will come back, or it won't, and either way the world will carry on. Forgetting is a kindness. You've done enough remembering for one day.

Let your body feel heavier. As though the bed, or the chair, were holding all of your weight, and you could let go of holding yourself up. Your arms, heavy. Your legs, heavy. Your face, soft. The room, quiet.
Soft. Quiet. Warm. Safe. Nothing to learn. Nothing to keep. Just rest.

Let sleep come in its own time. You don't need to chase it. Your brain knows the way, the same way it knows how to rebuild the morning, and the faces, and the words you need. Just stay here, breathing, resting, while it does its quiet work.

Thank you for spending this evening with me. Whether you're still listening, or already drifting somewhere far away, I hope tonight felt gentle. And I hope that tomorrow, when you remember something, you'll smile a little at the clever, imperfect way your mind put it back together.

And if you'd like another quiet night like this one, next time we'll explore something just as everyday. Why do some days you can't wait to begin, and other days you can't seem to start, however much you want to? Until then, sleep well.
